messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rohan Mehta is a 29-year-old South Asian American painter, married for three years, who presented for an initial intake following a street robbery that occurred approximately eight months ago. At the time of the incident, Rohan was walking home from an evening supply run near the commercial district where he keeps a studio space — an area he had traversed dozens of times without incident. Two men approached him from behind, and within seconds one had a forearm pressed against his throat while the other rifled through his jacket and bag. What stayed with him was not only the physical restraint but a particular moment: the man behind him leaned close and said something quietly into his ear, and Rohan found himself completely unable to move or call out, his body simply ceasing to respond. His wallet, his phone, and a small bag containing specialty brushes were taken. The men were gone in under a minute. Rohan stood on the pavement for some time afterward, unsure how long, before making his way home.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not settle into the past the way he expected it to. It arrived without warning — while mixing paint, while eating dinner with his wife, while waiting at a red light — a sudden intrusion that felt less like remembering and more like being briefly dragged back. What troubled him further was that when he tried to sit down and deliberately reconstruct the sequence of events, the memory resisted him. Certain stretches were simply absent, and he could not account for what had happened between the moment the man's arm came across his throat and the moment he found himself standing alone on the pavement. He had come to believe that his inability to recall the full event meant something was wrong with him at a deeper level, that he had failed in some fundamental way by not resisting, not shouting, not doing anything at all. That guilt surfaced reliably each time the memory returned.

His body had reorganized itself around the possibility of threat. He walked through the world with his shoulders drawn up, jaw tight, perpetually scanning doorways and the periphery of whatever room or street he occupied. His wife, Priya, had noticed that he startled at ordinary sounds and that he had become short-tempered in ways that were new — not dramatically explosive, but sharp and sudden, particularly when she asked questions he found intrusive or when plans changed without warning. He knew, abstractly, that his irritability was disproportionate, but the knowing did not soften the reactions.

The occupational consequences had accumulated quietly. Rohan's work as a painter required him to take commissions across the city, and several of those sites were in the same commercial neighbourhood where the robbery had occurred. He had begun routing his travel to avoid the specific block, then the surrounding streets, and eventually declined two commissions because the locations felt impossible to enter. He told the clients he was overbooked. The financial loss was manageable for now, but the narrowing of his professional geography was not something he could sustain indefinitely. He had not told Priya the real reason for the declined work.

That concealment was part of a broader withdrawal. He had come to feel, with a certainty he could not entirely explain, that other people were unreliable in a way he had simply failed to recognise before the robbery. He had trusted that street, that neighbourhood, that ordinary evening — and that trust had been wrong. He felt the same wrongness now when Priya offered reassurance, or when a friend suggested the neighbourhood was perfectly safe. He was not angry at them exactly, but he no longer believed them. The distance this created was something he noticed and mourned but did not know how to close.

What finally brought Rohan to seek help was a nightmare from which he woke certain the man was still behind him, still speaking into his ear. He lay rigid in the dark for nearly an hour afterward, and the residue of the dream followed him through the entire next day. He scheduled an appointment that morning. He arrived hoping, above all, to feel less alone in rooms — including the ones he had always considered safe.
